strengths: The core idea is simple, practical, and empirically effective: pessimistic (any-negative) aggregation over parallel verification queries, plus a chunk-based 'vertical' variant and a progressive combination, consistently improves TNR and balanced F1 across three benchmarks and roughly nine models of varying strength.

The finding that majority voting barely helps on verification while pessimistic aggregation does (Figure 3) is a genuinely useful and well-motivated observation, with a plausible explanation grounded in the error-detection bottleneck identified by Pandit et al. (2025).

The case study (Section 3.4, Table 1, Appendix A.3) is a valuable contribution: showing that many FN cases from strong verifiers correspond to real annotation errors in existing benchmarks is important for the community and is supported by concrete worked examples.

The new QiuZhen-Bench (1,054 advanced undergraduate/graduate-level problems from Yau Contest and Tsinghua qualifying exams) adds difficulty diversity beyond contest math, and the data-collection prompts are documented in the appendix.

Reproducibility is reasonably supported: full system/user prompts for both single-pass and chunk verification are provided in Appendix A.2, fixed settings (temperature 1.0, fixed reasoning effort) are stated, and code and dataset are linked.
weaknesses: Presentation quality is below the bar for a main-track submission: numerous typos and garbled symbols ('conpetitions', 'fron', 'drasticly', 'Prarllel', 'e0'/'e1' for ≠, '¡' for '<' in Case 3 comments), and all main results are reported only as dense multi-panel figures with no numeric tables, making exact numbers, variance, and model-by-model comparisons very hard to extract or verify.

Novelty is modest: any-negative/OR-style ensembling and chunked self-verification are fairly natural extensions of existing ideas; the authors themselves position the work as an extension of pessimistic verification (Liu et al., 2025), and the delta relative to that prior work and to agentic grading workflows (RefGrader, Mahdavi et al. 2025a) is not sharply delineated or empirically compared.

There is a potential circularity in the QiuZhen-Bench evaluation: labels are generated by GPT-5 with progressive@3/6 (the authors' own method) and human annotation effort appears limited to spot checks and a small FN review, so benchmark results on QiuZhen-Bench partially presuppose the method's reliability; the case-study evidence justifying GPT-5 annotation is based on only 13–20 FN cases per model, which is a very small sample for the claim that 'the majority' of FNs are annotation errors.

No statistical significance testing or confidence intervals are reported, and evaluation subsets are small (300 samples per benchmark), so several of the depicted gains (especially TPR drops of a few points) are hard to distinguish from noise.

The method's known cost—reduced TPR on correct proofs—is acknowledged but not deeply analyzed; there is little guidance on when the TNR/TPR tradeoff is favorable, limited ablation over the key hyperparameters (n, l, chunk size, pruning threshold), and the fixed progressive@3/6 setting appears chosen post hoc.

Baselines beyond single-pass long-CoT are thin: no comparison against other test-time verification strategies (debate, self-refine, RefGrader-style agentic grading, verifier training), so the claim of higher efficiency than 'scaling long-CoT' is established only against one alternative.
There is no dedicated limitations section, and some claims are overreached relative to evidence (e.g., 'near human experts', 'majority of false negatives are annotation errors').
